title: Bluetooth 7.0 specification ratified with HDT (High Data Throughput) support
summary: The Bluetooth SIG ratified the Bluetooth 7.0 specification on November 3, 2026, with the highlight of the new Bluetooth Core specification being optional support for HDT (High Data Throughput), delivering up to 7.5 Mbps bitrate. We first covered HDT in 2025 when initial/early support was implemented into the Ceva-Waves Links200 multi-protocol platform IP, and followed last September with the Realtek RTL8773J Bluetooth 7-ready Cortex-M55/M33 microcontroller. The main news is that the specification for Bluetooth 7.0 and the associated HDT feature is officially ratified/adopted. Bluetooth 7.0 highlights: Bluetooth High Data Throughput (HDT) introduces a new Bluetooth LE physical layer that increases the maximum Bluetooth bit rate to 7.5 Mbps while improving wireless efficiency and robustness. The higher bitrate is enabled by a combination of higher-order modulation, convolutional forward error correction, synchronization enhancements, adaptive rate selection, and enhanced packet architectures. It will be especially useful for high-resolution and lossless audio streaming. title: Web-based breadboard simulator lets you build circuits, fix errors, and monitor designs with a built-in oscilloscope
summary: Dev Kapadia s de:volt is a breadboard simulator that runs in your browser. You can place parts and wires on a breadboard, and the circuit runs live the whole time as you build it. The project aims to be as close as a real breadboard would be. It reports errors and warnings, and you can monitor pins with its built-in oscilloscope and/or multimeter. For instance, an LED with no resistor burns out, a weak battery sags under load, a motor pulls current, and a 555 on the 4-channel scope shows its timing capacitor charging and discharging. de:volt highlights: Build circuits on a virtual breadboard using the 105 parts available from the interface: resistors, capacitors, diodes, transistors, LEDs, 555 timers, 74-series and CD4000 logic, EEPROMs, motor drivers, sensors, and more. Four Arduino, BBC micro:bit, and RP2040 MCU boards are also available, and you can write and run MicroPython code from the web [...] The post Web-based breadboard simulator lets you build circuits, fix errors, and monitor designs with a built-in oscilloscope appeared first on CNX Software - Embedded Systems News .

title: Flipper One A Rockchip RK3576-powered portable Arm Linux computer and networking multi-tool (Crowdfunding)
summary: Flipper Devices has launched the Flipper One open-source hardware portable Arm Linux platform and networking/Edge AI multi-tool powered by a Rockchip RK3576 octa-core Arm Cortex-A72/A53 SoC. It also features a Raspberry Pi RP2350 microcontroller for low-level control. You may think of it as a successor to the popular STM32-based Flipper Zero hardware and wireless hacking tool, but the company stresses that the Flipper One is NOT a replacement for the Flipper Zero. It is a different product with mainline Linux kernel support, no binary blobs (probably not 100% true), and open-source drivers, and operating at a different level of the networking and wireless stacks with dual Gigabit Ethernet, Wi-Fi 6E, and optional 5G or 4G LTE modem.
